young.html: For parents: "A Rose for Emily" is a short, eerie story with a grim discovery at the end, usually read in high school. Young readers can learn here about how Faulkner tells a story out of order, and leave the story itself for later.
William Faulkner lived almost his whole life in a small town in Mississippi. He invented a whole imaginary county, with its own towns, families and history, and set most of his stories there.

In this story, the storyteller is not one person but a whole town, speaking as "we." The town tells what it remembers about a proud, lonely old woman, Miss Emily, but not in the order things happened. It jumps back and forth in time, the way people do when they gossip, and saves its biggest surprise for the end.

Tell it out of order. Think of a funny family story. Tell it starting at the end ("...and that's why there's a hole in the fence"), then jump back to the beginning, then the middle. Does starting at the end make people more curious? What does a storyteller gain by holding something back?

full.html: William Faulkner (1897–1962) spent most of his life in Oxford, Mississippi. He created Yoknapatawpha County, with its town of Jefferson, as the setting of novels such as The Sound and the Fury (1929) and As I Lay Dying (1930), and won the Nobel Prize in Literature for 1949. "A Rose for Emily," published in the magazine The Forum in April 1930, was his first short story in a national magazine and is now one of the most read American stories.
It opens at the end of a life:

full.text: When Miss Emily Grierson died, our whole town went to her funeral: the men through a sort of respectful affection for a fallen monument, the women mostly out of curiosity to see the inside of her house…
full.author: Faulkner
full.work: A Rose for Emily, section I
full.src: Literature in Context, University of Virginia

full.html: The "we" of the town then circles back through her life. Miss Emily is the last of a proud old family, kept from every suitor by her father. When he dies, she refuses for three days to admit it. Later she is seen with Homer Barron, a cheerful Northern foreman, and the town gossips. She buys poison without saying why; Homer disappears; a bad smell comes from her house, and the town's leaders, too polite to confront her, quietly sprinkle lime. She grows old alone, refusing to pay taxes or to accept the town's new ways.

full.text: Thus she passed from generation to generation—dear, inescapable, impervious, tranquil, and perverse.
full.author: Faulkner
full.work: A Rose for Emily, section IV
full.src: Literature in Context, University of Virginia

full.html: After her funeral, the townspeople open a room upstairs that no one has entered in forty years, and discover the dark secret of what happened to Homer Barron. The story ends on that discovery, which the lesson leaves undescribed.

full.name: gb-faulkner-order
full.cap: Switch between the order of telling and the order of events. Our summary.

full.html: Miss Emily stands for the Old South after the Civil War: proud, decaying and unable to let the past go. The town, which both reveres and spies on her, shares the blame for what it chose not to see.

The scrambled order is the story's engine. Because the town tells its memories out of sequence, readers gather clues without knowing they are clues, as the townspeople did, until the ending makes them fall into place.
Reading it only as a horror story. Faulkner said the "rose" of the title is a salute to a woman who had suffered, a small gesture of sympathy for her lonely, tragic life.

items: Dickens's Little Dorrit, earlier on this ladder, has its own decaying house and a woman shut away from time; Dickens's Miss Havisham, in Great Expectations, is another.
Cather's A Lost Lady and Fitzgerald's Gatsby, in this era, also show a community watching one figure as an old order passes.
Greek tragedy often uses a chorus that speaks for a community; Faulkner's "we" is a kind of chorus.
Twain's Huckleberry Finn, earlier on this ladder, is the other great portrait of the South on this ladder.
Why does the town never confront Miss Emily? What does politeness cost here?
What does it mean to be unable to let the past go?
Is the town a fair narrator? What does it get wrong?
How does telling events out of order change what we feel?

questions: The whole town tells this story. Why do you think Faulkner chose "we" instead of one narrator?
Why might people be afraid to ask a hard question?
Miss Emily refused to change with the times. When is it good to keep old ways, and when not?
What does the title's "rose" mean to you?
Have you ever pieced together a mystery from clues you noticed only later?
care: An eerie story that ends with a grim discovery about a man who disappeared years before; the lesson does not describe it. The story's opening sentence, shortened here, and a few later passages use racial language of its time; the lesson does not repeat it. For teens and adults.
